system.name: EMT
system.one_liner: an OS framework that lets Linux kernels support new, experimental hardware memory-translation architectures

components.name: Vanilla Linux
components.role: baseline column showing today's tightly-coupled memory-management stack

components.name: EMT-Linux
components.role: column showing Linux extended with the new EMT interface layer

components.name: VFS Interface
components.role: reference column showing the analogous, already-accepted file-system interface layer

components.name: Page Table Mgmt.
components.role: hardware-specific page-table code (linux/arch/*/mm/) directly coupled to Memory Mgmt. with no interface between them

components.name: MMU Hardware
components.role: the underlying hardware MMU a page-table implementation targets

components.name: EMT
components.role: the new proposed generic interface layer decoupling memory management from MMU-specific drivers

components.name: MMU Driver
components.role: hardware-specific driver implementing a given MMU design (Radix, ECPT, FPT, Hybrid) behind the EMT interface

components.name: System Calls
components.role: generic file-system system calls (read, fsync) that are hardware/format-neutral

components.name: VFS
components.role: the existing generic file-system interface layer, drawn as the analogy for EMT

components.name: File System
components.role: on-disk-format-specific file system implementation (Ext4, Btrfs) behind VFS

components.name: On-disk
components.role: on-disk data structures (Extent, B-tree) underlying a file system, the hardware-row analogy for MMU Hardware

components.name: Radix
components.role: the conventional radix-tree page-table format, the only option under vanilla Linux and one pluggable option under EMT

components.name: ECPT
components.role: the elastic cuckoo page table format, pluggable under EMT's MMU Driver

components.name: FPT
components.role: another pluggable page-table format under EMT's MMU Driver

components.name: Hybrid
components.role: a fourth pluggable page-table format under EMT's MMU Driver

content.key_idea: EMT inserts a generic interface layer, analogous to VFS in the file-system stack, between Linux's hardware-neutral memory-management code and hardware-specific MMU drivers, replacing vanilla Linux's tight, interface-less coupling with a pluggable Radix/ECPT/FPT/Hybrid driver model.
content.reading_order: Left to right across three columns (Vanilla Linux, EMT-Linux, VFS Interface), top to bottom within each column from the OS-level generic interface down to the hardware-specific driver and the hardware itself.

summary: This figure gives EMT's high-level design by comparing three column stacks: Vanilla Linux, EMT-Linux, and an analogous VFS Interface. In vanilla Linux, hardware-neutral Memory Mgmt. code is directly, tightly coupled ('No Interface') to hardware-specific Page Table Mgmt. code that only understands the Radix format running on MMU Hardware. EMT-Linux inserts a new generic EMT interface between Memory Mgmt. and a pluggable MMU Driver, letting Radix, ECPT, FPT, or Hybrid drivers sit underneath without changing the memory-management code above. The third column shows this is not a new idea: System Calls (read, fsync) already sit above the generic VFS interface, which itself sits above pluggable File System implementations (Ext4, Btrfs) over on-disk formats. The figure argues, by direct structural analogy, that EMT does for MMUs what VFS already does for file systems.
